To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

A. pallida larvae are capable of ingesting and internalizing Symbiodinium algae, and they can differentiate between compatible and incompatible alga strains, but only compatible algae are able to proliferate and become established within the host.

the specificity and timing for uptake and establishment of symbiosis in Aiptasia are similar in adult and larval animals and that compatible and incompatible Symbiodinium types can be distinguished by their ability to be internalized within host gastrodermal tissue.

Aiptasia adults, larvae, and cultured Symbiodinium cells have similar specificities for symbiont uptake, that the specificity of uptake is stable during long-term culture, and that compatible algae are internalized by host cells while incompatible algae are excluded.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the symbiotic interactions between corals and their symbiotic algae.
the symbiosis between reef-building corals and the photosynthetic microalgae that they host.
the cellular mechanisms that underpin the specificity and timing in the uptake of symbionts by the host, in the model system for coral research, Aiptasia, under controlled laboratory conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
A. sp1. larvae and adults show similar mechanisms of symbionts specificity.
the symbiosis is initiated in a similar manner in larvae and adults and that the specificity of symbiotic uptake is not affected by the age of the host or the stage of the life cycle.

(i) Aiptasia larvae are capable of taking up and retaining both compatible and incompatible strains of algae; (ii) only compatible algae are internalized by gastro-dermal cells, but this process is not necessarily linked with the uptake of algae by the gut; (iii) the uptake of compatible algae by gastrodermal cell does not appear to depend on the presence of incompatible algae in the gut; and (iv) the uptake of incompatible algae by larvae is reduced as the larvae age
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mechanisms of symbiosis initiation in anemone larvae appear to be similar to those in adult animals, and that the specificity of uptake of Symbiodinium by Aiptasia is determined by the algae rather than by the anemone.

we have shown that the specificity of symbiosis between Aiptasia and Symbiodinium is the same between adult and larval animals, and that this specificity is stable over time in the absence of host animals.
the specificity and timing for symbiosis onset is similar in Aiptasia larvae and adults and that the compatibility of symbionts is stable over time in axenic culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the symbiotic sea anemon Aiptasia can serve as an experimentally accessible model for the symbiotic coral-algae symbiosis.
we have developed a tractable experimental system that allows us to study the symbiosis in a controlled manner, which has been lacking in coral biology.
Aiptasia adults are not unique in their ability to distinguish between different types of algae.
